item.title: Nagasaki Events 2026: Lantern Festival, Kunchi & Shoro Nagashi
item.description: Nagasaki’s centuries as Japan’s window to China and the West shaped an event calendar unlike anywhere else in the country. The Lantern Festival fills the city with 15,000 Chinese lanterns each February; the Kunchi festival blends Japanese, Chinese, and Dutch influences into a spectacular autumn procession; and the deeply moving August 9 Peace Ceremony and the firecracker-lit Shoro Nagashi spirit boats give the summer a solemn power. This guide gathers the events worth planning a 2026 trip around, with a month-by-month calendar at the end.

item.title: Nagasaki Lantern Festival — Guide
item.description: The Nagasaki Lantern Festival, held over about two weeks around the Lunar New Year (late January to February), is the city’s most spectacular winter event, born from the Chinese New Year celebrations of Nagasaki’s Chinatown. During the festival some 15,000 red and multicoloured Chinese lanterns fill the streets, parks and river, bathing the whole city centre in a warm, festive glow after dark. Alongside them are huge illuminated figures and tableaux depicting Chinese legends and the zodiac, set up in the central plazas, plus nightly stage shows, lively dragon and lion dances, Chinese acrobatics and an emperor’s parade that fill the streets with music and colour.

item.title: Yamaga Lantern Festival — Guide
item.description: The Yamaga Lantern Festival (Yamaga Tōrō Matsuri), held every year on 15–16 August, is one of the most enchanting summer festivals in Japan. Its unforgettable highlight is the ‘Sennin Tōrō Odori’ — the Thousand-Person Lantern Dance — in which around a thousand women in matching summer yukata dance slowly and gracefully through the night, each balancing a delicate golden paper lantern (kintōrō), lit from within, on her head. As they move in unison to haunting music, the sea of soft golden lights weaving through the darkness creates a scene of extraordinary, dreamlike beauty.

item.title: Yamaguchi Chochin Lantern Festival — Guide
item.description: The Yamaguchi Gion Chochin Matsuri is the city’s great summer festival, a tradition some six hundred years old in which central Yamaguchi is lit by tens of thousands of glowing red paper lanterns. Strung in dense curtains along the main streets, over shrines and on lantern-decked poles and floats, their warm red light transforms the city into a magical scene after dark. The festivities include a lantern-lit dance in which performers move among the swaying lights, processions and shrine rites, all held over a couple of evenings in early August.

item.title: Kasuga Mantoro: The Lantern-Lighting of Kasuga Taisha — Guide
item.description: The Mantoro (literally ‘ten thousand lanterns’) is one of Nara’s most magical events, held at Kasuga Taisha twice a year — at Setsubun in early February and during Obon in mid-August. On these evenings, all of the shrine’s roughly 3,000 lanterns are lit at once: the some 2,000 moss-covered stone lanterns lining the forest approach and the around 1,000 bronze lanterns hanging from the vermilion halls, each flame an offering from worshippers over the centuries.

item.title: Higashiyama Hanatouro Guide: The Lantern Festival & What Replaced It
item.description: Important update: The Higashiyama Hanatouro festival has ended. Its final edition was held in March 2022, and the organisers concluded the event after roughly two decades. If you came looking for it, this guide explains what it was, why it stopped — and, more usefully, the beautiful evening illuminations and night temple visits you can still enjoy in Higashiyama today. For about twenty years, the Higashiyama Hanatouro (“flower and light path”) transformed eastern Kyoto into a magical evening promenade each March, lining the historic stone streets between Kiyomizu-dera and Maruyama Park with thousands of lanterns and seasonal flower displays.
